title: Intermittent FP16 accumulation bias during kernel hot-swap under adaptive batching
creator: Maya Chen
description: Summary: While rolling out the adaptive kernel hot-swap path to reduce tail latency, we observed intermittent numerical drift in long-sequence decoding runs. The drift presents as a small but growing bias in FP16 accumulator values that leads to softmax instability and token distribution skew after ~1500 decode steps. This ticket tracks the investigation and proposed mitigation.
steps_to_repro: 1) Deploy runtime binary with kernel-hot-swap feature flag enabled (hot-swap = on, adaptive_batching = aggressive)
2) Run the regression harness: python tests/regressions/long_sequence_decode.py --model=xgen-13b --seq_len=2048 --batch_size=8 --tokens=1600 --retries=20
3) Observe divergence metric in tests/metrics/divergence.log and intermittent softmax NaN or large-prob jumps in decode traces
4) Reproduce more reliably when GPU utilization > 80% and persistent kernel handoffs occur (kernel A -> kernel B on warmup path)
5) Attach --enable-kv-cache=true to increase stateful pressure and speed up divergence
observed_behavior: After ~1200-1800 decode steps, model outputs start to diverge from baseline: top-k token probabilities shift by 0.03-0.12 L1 distance. Occasional softmax values saturate causing token repetition. Logs occasionally show non-zero 'accum_state' on kernel entry after hot-swap.
expected_behavior: Numerical outputs should remain within deterministic tolerance of baseline (L1 < 0.005) for identical seeds and inputs. Kernel hot-swap should transfer execution without leaving stale accumulator state.

investigation_findings:
Preliminary root-cause hypothesis: when we perform kernel hot-swap under high batching pressure, the accumulator buffer used for attention accumulation (FP16) is not being fully zeroed/reinitialized for the incoming kernel variant. Two contributing factors found:
- scheduler uses a racey heartbeat to preempt and migrate in-flight batches; the lifecycle hooks assume the outgoing kernel will clear shared accum buffers but there are code paths where it returns ownership without zeroing.
- new fused attention kernel (kernel.B) uses an aliasing buffer view for accumulator to avoid an extra allocation; when it maps onto the same slab as the previous kernel variant, stale FP16 residuals remain and get added into subsequent reductions, causing monotonic bias (small positive offset).
Reproduction correlates with: high GPU utilization, large KV cache footprints, and sequence lengths > 1024. Unit tests with deterministic single-kernel runs pass; issue only appears across hot-swap boundary.
root_cause: Race between scheduler hot-swap finalizer and kernel teardown + buffer aliasing optimization in kernel.B. The finalizer assumes kernel-owned accumulator has been zeroed by teardown; kernel.B trusted a shared slab and performed lazy zeroing only on write, letting tiny FP16 denorms persist when write paths are short-circuited by prefetch heuristics.
fix_proposal: 1) Short-term: Explicitly zero accumulator slab on kernel-entry path as a safe guard (adds one memclear) and disable aliasing heuristic under hot-swap_enabled flag. 2) Medium-term: Add ownership transfer handshake to scheduler that atomically revokes buffer aliases before kernel swap completes. 3) Add unit/integration tests to simulate hot-swap with aggressive batching and KV cache pressure; assert accumulators are cleared. 4) Add telemetry metric 'accum_nonzero_on_entry' and an alert for >0.1% rate.
work_done:
- Reproduced locally on test cluster with harness and captured logs (see linked PR).
- Built instrumented runtime with 'accum-probe' enabled to count non-zero accumulator entries.
- Drafted initial non-zero guard patch (memclear on entry) and validated it prevents divergence on the regression harness in 20/20 runs.
next_steps: 1) Open internal RFC for scheduler ownership handshake and buffer aliasing semantics (owner: scheduler team)
2) Land hotfix memclear + feature-flag rollback path (PR: see linked_prs) and enable on canary cluster
3) Add integration test in CI that runs long_sequence_decode against both kernel variants under hot-swap flag
4) Monitor accum_nonzero_on_entry telemetry for 72h after canary rollout
5) Follow-up: design a lower-cost zeroing strategy (page-level tombstone or write barrier) to avoid full memclear perf regression
